# On ones and on twos

Both 24 and 12 work, and the difference has a name.

- **On ones:** a new drawing on every frame. 24 drawings fill one second.
- **On twos:** each drawing stays on screen for two frames. 12 drawings fill one second.

![Two rows of 12 frames, the first half second: on ones, a new drawing in every frame; on twos, each drawing held for two frames](asset:ones_and_twos)

**Your assignment is on twos.** The 12 dots on your chart become 12 drawings, each held for two frames. That makes 24 frames: one second.

**Why 24?** Not because your eye needs 24. In 1926, as sound came to film, engineers at Western Electric needed one fixed speed so recorded voices would not warble. They picked roughly the average speed theaters already ran.

{{deeper}}

**If you picked 6,** you found a real practice too. Some styles hold each drawing for four frames ("on fours"). It looks choppier, and when it is done on purpose it is a style, not a mistake. For smooth motion, 24 or 12 is the answer.

**On twos is a choice, not a shortcut.** Most classic hand-drawn animation is on twos. The held frame gives the eye a moment to land, and a lot of animation looks crisper on twos than on ones. Very fast action often goes on ones, because on twos it can flicker.

**Before sound,** silent films had no fixed speed, and theaters sped them up or slowed them down. On twos, 12 drawings a second, is built on the number the sound engineers chose.
